```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

oxidizr computes carbohydrate (CHO), fat and protein oxidation from VO2, VCO2
and urea excretion. Its coefficients are not typed in: the package derives
them from balanced oxidation reactions when it is built. The method follows
chapter 1 of Telmosse (2022), which writes out every step of indirect
respiratory calorimetry and of the 13C tracer calculation. This vignette gives
the reactions, the constants, and the reasons for each choice, with the
sources the thesis cites. Page numbers refer to Telmosse (2022).

```{r setup}
library(oxidizr)
```

## Principle

Indirect respiratory calorimetry rests on two kinds of input: VO2 and VCO2
measured at the mouth, plus urea or nitrogen excreted in urine and possibly
sweat (Lemon & Mullin, 1980). It also rests on the stoichiometry of the
aerobic oxidation of the substrates (Livesey & Elia, 1988). The thesis writes
this stoichiometry for three reference substrates: glucose, a representative
triacylglycerol (TAG) and a representative protein (p. 17).

For 1 g of each substrate, k is the volume of O2 used and l the volume of CO2
produced. With P the protein oxidized and m the urea produced per gram of
protein, the system is (pp. 23-26):

$$VO_2 = k_1\,CHO + k_2\,FAT + k_3\,P \qquad VCO_2 = l_1\,CHO + l_2\,FAT + l_3\,P \qquad urea = m\,P$$

Because glucose has an RQ of 1 (k1 = l1), subtracting the two gas equations
gives FAT directly; CHO follows from the VO2 equation. `gas_yield()` computes
k and l from a molecular formula, and `stoich_coefficients` holds the solution:

```{r}
round(unlist(stoich_coefficients), 4)
```

These are the defaults of `calc_substrate_oxidation()`:
CHO = `cho_vco2` VCO2 + `cho_vo2` VO2 and
FAT = `fat_vo2` VO2 + `fat_vco2` VCO2, after removal of the protein share of
VO2 and VCO2.

## Gas volumes and atomic weights

The thesis takes one mole of O2 or CO2 at STPD as 22.4 L and rounds atomic
weights to 12, 1, 16 and 14 g/mol for C, H, O and N (p. 17). It notes that
O2 and CO2 are not ideal gases and cites the real molar volumes of Péronnet &
Massicotte (1991), 22.3858 L for O2 and 22.2966 L for CO2, but does not use
them (p. 17).

oxidizr uses 22.414 L/mol for both gases, the ideal-gas value of Livesey &
Elia (1988), with the atomic weights of Péronnet & Massicotte (1991, Table 1).
The molar volume has a larger effect than the choice of lipid (next sections):
with the real-gas volumes, glucose has an RQ of 0.996 instead of 1.

```{r}
glucose <- c(C = 6, H = 12, O = 6)
volumes <- list(
  "22.4 L/mol" = 22.4,
  "22.414 L/mol (Livesey & Elia, 1988)" = 22.414,
  "Real gases (Péronnet & Massicotte, 1991)" = c(O2 = 22.3858, CO2 = 22.2966)
)
t(sapply(volumes, function(v) round(gas_yield(glucose, molar_volume = v), 4)))
```

All rows use the atomic weights of Péronnet & Massicotte (1991), so the
22.4 L/mol row gives 0.7460 L/g; the thesis obtains 0.747 L/g with a molar
mass of 180 g/mol (p. 20).

## Carbohydrate: glucose

C6H12O6 + 6 O2 → 6 CO2 + 6 H2O

The thesis treats the choice of carbohydrate as simple, because glucose is
the main simple carbohydrate, both as ingested and as stored (p. 42). Its
storage forms, starch and glycogen, are polymers of glucosyl units
(C6H10O5)n. Per glucosyl unit, glycogen uses 0.830 L O2/g, produces the same
volume of CO2 and yields 4.18 kcal/g (pp. 42-43). The equations can use
either form (p. 43).

Two arguments make the choice of little practical importance. First, glucose
formed from amino acids or glycerol is only an intermediate: VO2, VCO2 and,
for amino acids, nitrogen output are the same whether a substrate is oxidized
directly or after conversion to glucose. Indirect calorimetry sees only the
net balance (Livesey & Elia, 1988; pp. 43-44). Second, the thesis concludes
that there is no point in arguing whether CHO oxidation should be expressed
as grams of glucose or grams of glycogen (p. 44).

For the same reason, it does not follow Jeukendrup & Wallis (2005), who
proposed different CHO equations for different exercise intensities. The
shares of plasma glucose and muscle glycogen do change with intensity, but
only isotope tracers can measure them (McCue & Welch, 2016). If they are
measured, two equations are not necessary (Kipp et al., 2018); if they are
not, there is no way to know whether the intensity-specific estimates are
correct (p. 44). oxidizr therefore expresses CHO oxidation in grams of
glucose.

## Lipid: the TAG-type C53.4H99.2O6

C53.4H99.2O6 + 75.2 O2 → 53.4 CO2 + 49.6 H2O

Each triacylglycerol is made of three fatty acids, drawn from about forty in
humans and bound to glycerol in a random arrangement (Berry et al., 1986;
Livesey & Elia, 1988). Calorimetry therefore needs one formula that stands
for the TAGs most often oxidized, a "TAG-type" (p. 20). The thesis uses
C53.4H99.2O6 because it matches the coefficients of the Institute of Medicine
(2005): RQ 0.71 and 9.44 kcal/g. The atom counts are not whole numbers
because the formula stands for a mixture (p. 20). With 22.4 L/mol and
836 g/mol, it uses 2.015 L O2/g and produces 1.431 L CO2/g (p. 21).

The thesis then argues that the exact formula cannot be known (pp. 45-46):

- Human TAGs contain seven main fatty acids in variable proportions
  (Livesey & Elia, 1988), and nothing shows which ones lipolysis releases.
- Adipose-tissue lipolysis seems to release fewer than three fatty acids per
  glycerol, which points to incomplete lipolysis or re-esterification
  (Björntorp et al., 1969). The fatty acids released can then differ from the
  TAGs that store them.
- The fatty acids that muscle oxidizes need not match those released by
  adipose tissue.
- The mean composition of adipose-tissue TAGs is fairly well known (Livesey &
  Elia, 1988), but intramuscular TAGs, which supply much of the fat used in
  exercise, are poorly documented: their composition, release and oxidation
  (Havel et al., 1967).

Earlier authors used different lipids (p. 48, Table 2): Frayn (1983) and
Ferrannini (1988) used palmitoyl-stearoyl-oleoyl-glycerol, C55H104O6;
Péronnet & Massicotte (1991) and Jeukendrup & Wallis (2005) used a mean fatty
acid, C17.2702H32.7142O2. The thesis simulated the published equations over
an RQ of 0.85 to 1.0 and a VO2 of 0.3 to 4.0 L/min. The differences in CHO
and fat oxidation, energy expenditure and energy shares were small at every
RQ (pp. 49-52). It concludes that the choice of lipid has neither theoretical
interest, because the questions above have no answer, nor practical interest
(p. 46).

The table below repeats the comparison at VO2 = 2.50 and VCO2 = 2.30 L/min
(RER 0.92), all at 22.414 L/mol. It adds dioleoyl-palmitoyl-glycerol, the
reference fat of Livesey & Elia (1988, Table 4: RQ 0.7097, 39.5 kJ/g); this
row is not in the thesis.

```{r}
lipids <- list(
  "TAG-type (Telmosse, 2022)" = c(C = 53.4, H = 99.2, O = 6),
  "Palmitoyl-stearoyl-oleoyl-glycerol (Frayn, 1983)" = c(C = 55, H = 104, O = 6),
  "Dioleoyl-palmitoyl-glycerol (Livesey & Elia, 1988)" = c(C = 55, H = 102, O = 6),
  "Mean fatty acid (Péronnet & Massicotte, 1991)" = c(C = 17.2702, H = 32.7142, O = 2)
)
glc <- gas_yield(glucose)
compare <- t(sapply(lipids, function(f) {
  fat <- gas_yield(f)
  k <- solve(rbind(c(glc[["o2"]], fat[["o2"]]), c(glc[["co2"]], fat[["co2"]])))
  ox <- k %*% c(2.50, 2.30)
  c(L_O2_per_g = fat[["o2"]], L_CO2_per_g = fat[["co2"]],
    RQ = fat[["co2"]] / fat[["o2"]], CHO_g_min = ox[1], fat_g_min = ox[2])
}))
knitr::kable(compare, digits = 4)
```

## Protein

The body holds thousands of proteins, so the calculation also needs a
representative "protein-type" (Livesey & Elia, 1988; p. 21). The thesis uses
C89H148.5O32N23.5 because it matches the coefficients of the Institute of
Medicine (2005) (p. 21). Its nitrogen leaves as urea:

C89H148.5O32N23.5 + 92.5 O2 → 77.25 CO2 + 50.75 H2O + 11.75 CO(NH2)2

At 22.4 L/mol and 2057.5 g/mol, this gives 1.0070 L O2/g, 0.8410 L CO2/g and
an RQ of 0.835 (p. 22). Table 1 of the thesis lists 1.0075 and 0.8443 L/g
(p. 18), the values that earlier versions of oxidizr used. Oxidation of one
mole gives 11.75 × 60 = 705 g of urea, that is 0.343 g of urea per g of
protein, or 2.915 g of protein per g of urea; with 16% nitrogen, 1 g of
nitrogen stands for 6.25 g of protein (p. 22). Sulfur from cysteine and
methionine is ignored, because it is a small part of protein mass and cannot
be measured independently (p. 22). As for lipids, the thesis judges that the
choice of protein formula has neither theoretical nor practical interest
(p. 48).

oxidizr takes the general protein values of Livesey & Elia (1988, Table 6),
which the Institute of Medicine (2005) repeats: 19.68 kJ/g divided by
19.48 kJ/L O2 gives 1.0103 L O2/g; with an RQ of 0.835, 0.8436 L CO2/g. The
urea factor is 6.25 g of protein per g of nitrogen (Livesey & Elia, 1988,
p. 620) times the nitrogen fraction of urea (0.46646), 2.9154 g of protein
per g of urea.

The thesis also describes how protein oxidation is measured (pp. 52-53).
Complete calorimetry needs urea excretion in urine and sweat, but in short
tests urine and sweat production is too small to measure it reliably. When
urine and sweat cannot be collected, an average protein oxidation can be
assumed, if the experimental situation does not change it (Romijn et al.,
1992). This correction is acceptable when energy expenditure rises only a
little; when it rises a lot, protein oxidation increases and the correction
becomes less exact (Tarnopolsky et al., 1995). Urinary nitrogen tends to overestimate
protein oxidation, because not all of it comes from protein. In exercise
studies where protein contributes little energy, protein oxidation is often
set to zero ("non-protein" calorimetry). The thesis notes that this is false
in principle, but that the error on estimated energy expenditure is under 1%
(p. 53). `calc_sweat_loss()`, `calc_urea_loss()` and `calc_protein_oxidation()`
implement the urine and sweat balance.

## Energy per gram

The energy factors are the heats of combustion of the Institute of Medicine
(2005, Table 5-1), reproduced in the thesis (Table 1, p. 18; Figure 2, p. 19):

```{r}
unlist(energy_factors)
```

They repeat Livesey & Elia (1988): glucose 15.56 kJ/g (Table 2), general fat
39.5 kJ/g and protein 19.68 kJ/g (Table 6, for N excreted as urea, ammonia
and creatinine in the ratio 90:5:5). The IOM table
credits the protein value of 4.7 kcal/g to Livesey & Elia (1988).

## Exogenous glucose oxidation with 13C

A 13C balance on expired CO2 gives the oxidation of ingested glucose, G
(g/min). The CO2 from exogenous glucose, k × G, carries the enrichment of the
drink, Rexo; the rest carries the background enrichment, Rendo (pp. 66-67):

$$VCO_2\,R_{exp} = k\,G\,R_{exo} + (VCO_2 - k\,G)\,R_{endo} \quad\Rightarrow\quad G = \frac{VCO_2\,(R_{exp} - R_{endo})}{k\,(R_{exo} - R_{endo})}$$

This is the Mosora equation. Mosora et al. (1976) first presented the
principle, the name comes from Mosora et al. (1981), Jandrain et al. (1989)
showed the equation and Péronnet et al. (1990) derived it (p. 68). k is the
CO2 produced per gram of glucose. The thesis uses 6 × 22.4 / 180 = 0.747 L/g
(p. 20); oxidizr computes it from the same glucose reaction:

```{r}
stoich_coefficients$co2_cho_ratio
```

The thesis notes that atom fractions (13C/C) are strictly correct and ratios
(13C/12C) are not, but that the difference is negligible at these enrichments
(p. 68).

**Background enrichment.** The 13C content of expired CO2 rises by up to 1‰
PDB from rest to exercise, because glycogen is slightly richer in 13C than
TAGs and its share of VCO2 rises with intensity (Schoeller et al., 1980;
Massicotte et al., 1993; Bergman & Brooks, 1999). A resting Rendo therefore
overestimates exogenous glucose oxidation (p. 70). The thesis lists four
remedies (pp. 71-73): take Rendo from an exercise trial without exogenous
glucose (Pallikarakis et al., 1986); measure with two enrichments and solve
for G and Rendo (Péronnet et al., 1990); use a high artificial enrichment of
20 to 100‰ PDB, which makes the drift negligible (Burelle et al., 1997); or
use 14C, now avoided for ethical reasons (Beckers et al., 1994). In oxidizr,
`calc_rref()` takes Rref from the control protocol, which is the first remedy.

**CO2 recovery.** At rest, only 50 to 80% of labelled bicarbonate appears as
13CO2 at the mouth (Costill et al., 1973; Wolfe & Jahoor, 1990), because about
50 mL/min of CO2 exchanges with a large, slow bone pool (Pallikarakis et al.,
1991a). During exercise at a VO2 of 3 L/min, this exchange is under 2% of
VCO2, and recovery is practically 100% (Ruzzin et al., 2003; Trimmer et al.,
2001; pp. 75-76).
oxidizr therefore applies no recovery correction.

**Delay.** Labelled CO2 passes through the slowly renewed bicarbonate pool, so
breath enrichment rises with a half-life of 30 to 40 min; about 40 min are
needed to reach equilibrium (Pallikarakis et al., 1991a). The thesis excludes
data before 40 min of exercise (p. 77). In oxidizr, use `time_range`, for
example `analyze_oxidation(study, time_range = c(40, 120))`.

**RER above 1.** In intense exercise or metabolic acidosis, hyperventilation
releases CO2 from the bicarbonate pool and the RQ at the mouth can exceed 1.0.
Indirect calorimetry is then not valid (Frayn, 1983; Ferrannini, 1988;
Jeukendrup & Wallis, 2005; pp. 56-57). oxidizr sets negative oxidation rates
to 0, so fat oxidation is 0 above an RER of 1. `validate_study()` warns above
an RER of 1.05 and reports an error above 1.10.
